questions.explain: The pool is keyed by the exact connection string — even a trailing space creates a separate pool. Identical strings share one pool, so the guidance is to use identical connection strings everywhere and never build them dynamically per user.
options: It opens a new physical connection for every application thread.
It is keyed by the exact connection string — identical connection strings share a pool, and any difference (even a trailing space) creates a separate pool.
Pooling is done server-side by SQL Server's thread pool.
Pools are shared automatically across all application servers in the fleet.
questions.q: How does ADO.NET/SqlClient connection pooling key its pools, and what follows from that?

questions.explain: sp_reset_connection clears most session state — temp tables are dropped, SET options revert, open transactions roll back. Applications relying on session-level state surviving across Open/Close boundaries will break under pooling.
options: Temp tables are dropped, open transactions roll back, and most SET options revert.
Only the connection password is cleared; all session state persists.
It forces a full re-authentication with the domain controller.
It terminates the pool and forces all clients to reconnect.
questions.q: When a pooled connection is reset between checkouts, what happens to session-level state via sp_reset_connection?

questions.explain: Register the remote with sp_addlinkedserver, map logins with sp_addlinkedsrvlogin, then query with four-part names. OPENQUERY sends a literal SQL string to the remote side and is preferred when the optimizer won't push filters down effectively.
options: Register with sp_addlinkedserver and map logins with sp_addlinkedsrvlogin; use four-part names, or OPENQUERY to force pass-through SQL when the optimizer fails to push filters down.
Create a foreign data wrapper with CREATE SERVER and import the remote schema.
Linked servers are configured in the connection string of the client application.
Use BULK INSERT against the remote server's file system.
questions.q: How do you set up and query a SQL Server linked server, and when should you prefer OPENQUERY?

questions.explain: CDC is enabled per table with sys.sp_cdc_enable_table and reads the transaction log to emit row-level changes — more efficient and accurate than timestamp polling (which needs updated_at on every table and can't capture deletes). Captured tables need primary keys.
options: It captures changes with triggers on every table.
It is enabled per table with sys.sp_cdc_enable_table and reads the transaction log to emit row-level changes; tables need primary keys.
It requires the database to be in SIMPLE recovery model.
It polls tables using updated_at timestamps on a schedule.
questions.q: Which statement about SQL Server Change Data Capture (CDC) is TRUE?

questions.explain: Add the new column alongside the old one and write to both (expand), update downstream consumers, then drop the old column once no consumer references it (contract) — decoupling the database migration from downstream deployment timelines.
options: Rename the column in place during a maintenance window and update all consumers simultaneously.
Expand/contract: add the new column alongside the old one, write to both, migrate consumers, then drop the old column once nothing references it.
Use SELECT * in all integration queries so new columns appear automatically.
Drop and recreate the table with the new schema during the ETL load.
questions.q: What is the expand/contract pattern for schema changes across integration boundaries?
